messages.content: I enjoy walking with my friend, but talking the whole time tires me out.
You might try letting some stretches be quiet, with the occasional observation when something catches your eye.
Would silence seem unfriendly?
It could feel unfamiliar, but it doesn't have to be unfriendly. You could say you enjoy walking together even when you're quiet.
My friend is quite talkative, though.
You could mention that you sometimes need a quiet stretch, while still making room for conversation at other points.
What could I say without making it sound like a complaint?
Maybe: “I enjoy our walks. Talking the whole time can tire me out, so would you mind if we had some quiet stretches too?”
What can readers infer about the setting? “Rain tapped the tin roof. Under a single lamp, Imani sorted letters on a wooden counter. A bell rang as the door opened.”
The passage mentions rain, a tin roof, a lamp, a wooden counter and a door. It may be a shop or office, but the passage doesn't establish which.
Is it definitely nighttime?
No. The passage mentions a lamp, but doesn't say what time it is.
Could it be a post office?
Possibly: sorting letters on a counter fits that reading, though it doesn't confirm the place.
What about the weather?
It's raining in the scene; the passage doesn't say how heavy the rain is.
Does the bell tell us someone entered?
The door opened and a bell rang. Someone may have entered, but that isn't stated.
I want to keep the location ambiguous.
You can retain the counter and letters without naming the building; those details allow several possibilities.
What's a useful unanswered question?
A reader might wonder who or what opened the door.
Give me another that concerns the place.
“What kind of building is Imani in?”
For our mural, I sketched the outline, Dev mixed the colours, and Sal painted the birds. Who did what?
You sketched the outline, Dev mixed the colours, and Sal painted the birds.
Who painted the background?
Your account doesn't say who painted it.
I'm writing a caption. Can I credit Dev with the background?
Only if you have that information elsewhere. Your account credits Dev with mixing colours, but doesn't say who painted the background.
Draft a caption using only these contributions.
“I sketched the outline, Dev mixed the colours, and Sal painted the birds.”
Make it sound less like a list.
“With my sketched outline and colours mixed by Dev, the mural features birds painted by Sal.”
Does that assign anyone the background?
No. It doesn't say who painted the background.

Make the second paragraph more conversational. First: “The meeting begins at noon. Attendance is optional.” Second: “Participants may submit questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.”
Second paragraph: “You can send questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.”
Could the first bit sound warmer?
Do you mean the first paragraph, or the first part of my revised second paragraph?
The first part of the revised second paragraph.
You could say: “Feel free to send questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.”
Keep it conversational, but less inviting.
“You can send questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.”
Can you avoid “ahead of time”?
It's already avoided: “You can send questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.”
Does that still say when answers come?
Yes. It says the responses will be provided during the session.
Make just the first sentence of my original first paragraph conversational too.
“The meeting starts at noon.”
Put both revised parts together, leaving the other sentence alone.

The meeting starts at noon. Attendance is optional.

You can send questions in advance. Responses will be provided during the session.
How do because and so connect ideas?
“Because” introduces a reason; “so” introduces a result. For example: “I stayed in because it rained” and “It rained, so I stayed in.”
Does the reason have to come first?
No. With “because,” either order works: “Because it rained, I stayed in” or “I stayed in because it rained.”
My sentence is: I left early because I felt tired.
The reason is feeling tired; the result is leaving early.
Can you use so?
“I felt tired, so I left early.”
Does that change the cause?
No. Feeling tired remains the reason for leaving early.
Can I start with because and keep the same meaning?
Yes: “Because I felt tired, I left early.”
Which version is shorter?
All three versions have seven words.
